html:
The Afrasiyab murals are wall paintings from the 7th century found in 1965 at Afrasiyab, the hill of old Samarkand in today's Uzbekistan. They are among the finest works of art left by the Sogdians.

They decorated a hall in the residence of Varkhuman, king of Samarkand around the 650s and 660s. A Sogdian inscription on one wall describes envoys coming to him. The paintings show a crowded scene of visitors from many lands bringing gifts:

  • Chinese officials, and a Tang princess in a boat
  • two Korean envoys, probably from Goguryeo, with feathers in their caps
  • Turkic guards with long braided hair, from the Türk Khaganates
  • envoys from nearby Central Asian states

Chinese records name Varkhuman too: the Tang emperor Gaozong made him governor of the region, at the height of Tang power in the west. The murals show Sogdia as a crossroads of Silk Road diplomacy, just before the Arab conquest of the early 8th century brought Islam.
